items.stem: For N divisible by n, the systematic interval is:
items.explanation: The interval is the frame size divided by the sample size.

items.stem: In the standard linear design, the random start is selected from:
items.explanation: The start is selected uniformly from the first k positions.

items.stem: For N=nk, the first-order inclusion probability is:
items.explanation: Each unit is selected by exactly one of the k possible starts.

items.stem: A major risk of systematic sampling is:
options: The sample always has unequal size
items.explanation: A repeating frame pattern can align with the fixed interval.

items.stem: How many possible samples exist when N=nk?
items.explanation: There is one systematic sample for each possible start.

items.stem: Successive positions are obtained by:
items.explanation: The fixed interval is added to obtain each successive position.

items.stem: N=20 and n=4. Find k.
items.explanation: k=20/4=5. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.

items.stem: N=20, n=4, r=3. List selected positions.
items.explanation: Start at 3 and add 5 to obtain 3,8,13,18.

items.stem: For N=20 and n=4, π_i is:
items.explanation: π_i=n/N=4/20=1/5. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.

items.stem: For distinct units in different residue classes modulo k, π_ij is:
items.explanation: They cannot occur together under any single random start.

items.stem: N=36 and n=6. How many possible starts exist?
items.explanation: k=36/6=6; there are six starts. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.

items.stem: Which statements about linear systematic sampling are true?
items.explanation: A, B and D are true. Linear systematic sampling selects one of the k possible systematic samples, not every subset of size n.
statements: A random start is selected from the k possible starting positions.
After the start, every k-th unit is selected.
Every subset of n units is equally likely under linear systematic sampling.
When N/n is integral, the sampling interval is k=N/n.

A.why: The random start gives each of the k possible systematic samples its design probability.

B.why: The fixed interval determines the subsequent selected positions.

C.why: Only the systematic samples generated by the possible starts can be selected; arbitrary subsets are not all possible.

D.why: For an integral interval, dividing frame size by sample size gives k.

items.stem: The four possible sample means are 3,5,7,9. Find their design mean.
items.explanation: (3+5+7+9)/4=6. The calculation follows the stated sampling formula; identify the relevant population and sample quantities before interpreting the result.
items.check: Average equally over the four starts.

items.stem: For possible sample means 3,5,7,9, find design variance.
items.explanation: Mean is 6; average squared deviations (9+1+1+9)/4=5.

items.stem: Which statements about systematic variance estimation are correct?
items.explanation: A, C and D are correct. The single-start limitation is a central reason systematic sampling variance estimation needs care.
statements: A single random start usually provides limited direct information about design variance.
One systematic sample always gives an unbiased variance estimator without extra assumptions.
A suitable frame order can create implicit stratification.
Periodicity in the frame can interact with the sampling interval and affect precision.

A.why: Only one of the possible systematic samples is observed, so direct design-variance estimation is difficult.

B.why: A single start does not generally identify the design variance without additional assumptions or replication.

C.why: Ordering similar units together can spread the sample across the frame.

D.why: A periodic pattern aligned with k can produce an unusually unrepresentative sample.

items.stem: Two distinct units can have π_ij=1/k when:
options: Their positions are congruent modulo k
They are both in the first half
items.explanation: Units in the same residue class occur together for one start.

items.stem: N=8 and n=2. How many possible systematic samples are there?
items.explanation: k=8/2=4, so there are four possible starts.
items.check: The number of starts equals k.

items.stem: Why can systematic sampling be operationally attractive?
options: It spreads selected units through an ordered frame
It makes all pairs have positive π_ij
items.explanation: The fixed interval can provide a spread-out sample.

items.stem: Equal first-order inclusion probabilities imply:
items.explanation: Variance also depends on joint inclusion probabilities and the sample space.

items.stem: If a frame repeats every six entries and k=6, the main concern is:
items.explanation: The repeating pattern aligns with the interval.
